description:
We are a designer and a developer willing to explore new ways to interact with technology.
We are interested in creating phydigital experiences. With this project we aim to create a new way for people to interact with data. 
And we are looking for someone with music or sound, arts and humanistic experience.
We welcome people who feel creative and inspired about this challenge.
summary:
HEARTH (Hear the Earth) is a multisensory installation and an immersive experience that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into real-time soundscapes. It works in any browser and is also designed for Meta Quest headsets. Users choose an EIC visualization and step into its 3D spatial soundscape. Computer vision analyzes the frames, and visual features drive the audio: color becomes harmony, pixel density becomes rhythm, and movement becomes melody. 

All mappings are constrained to musical scales, so the result is beautiful rather than noisy, while subtle patterns in the data stay audible.

In museums and planetariums, HEARTH becomes a physical space. NASA’s visualizations are projected around visitors while 3D sound, smells, air intensity, and temperature respond to what they see, so people can touch, move, listen, and feel how our planet changes.

HEARTH invites everyone, not only blind and low-vision users, to connect with the data and with the Earth through their senses, because sight alone can hide patterns that other senses catch. When everyone can feel our planet, they connect, they get involve and help to protect it.
details:
What it does and how it works

HEARTH turns NASA visualizations into 3D spatial soundscapes you can walk through. The user enters the ID of any visualization from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio (the number in its svs.gsfc.nasa.gov address) and presses “Listen”. HEARTH loads the visualization, analyzes the image with computer vision, and places the result in an immersive 3D scene where an avatar explores the data while sound responds to what it finds. Different regions and data types are voiced with different instruments, percussion, and sound effects. Everything is constrained to musical scales, so the result is pleasant to hear while subtle patterns in the data stay audible. A built-in parameters panel lets users change how the image is read and how it sounds, and share their settings as JSON. The web app runs in any browser and is built to run in Meta Quest headsets, where visitors can stand inside the soundscape.

Benefits

- It makes Earth science accessible to blind and low-vision users, with screen-reader compatibility, descriptive audio text, and simple navigation.

- It is not only for blind users. It gives everyone a new way to connect with data and with the Earth through their senses, and the ear can catch patterns the eye misses.

- It works with any NASA SVS visualization, so the library grows with NASA’s catalog.

- It needs nothing to install: open a link in a browser or a headset.

Intended impact

We want people to better understand data and feel the changes in our planet, not only see them. HEARTH builds an emotional connection with our home planet and makes climate science inclusive, multisensory, and global. It aids scientific dissemination by turning NASA’s visualizations into experiences that anyone can open with a link, so Earth science can reach far beyond people who already follow it.

HEARTH is meant for scientists, museums, planetariums, schools, and the general public. It helps blind and low-vision people explore Earth data independently. It also gives everyone a new way to connect with data through their senses, since the ear can catch patterns the eye misses. The same engine can power a physical multisensory installation, where NASA’s visualizations are projected around visitors while 3D sound, smells, air intensity, and temperature respond to what they see. When everyone can understand Earth, everyone can help protect it.

Tools and technologies

• Data and visuals: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) visualizations tied to the Earth Information Center themes, loaded through the SVS API.

• Web and 3D: a web application built with JavaScript, Node.js, and three.js, with spatial audio (Web Audio API), deployed on Render. It runs in any browser and adds a VR mode (WebXR) for Meta Quest headsets.

• Analysis: image analysis of each visualization (color ranges and their density across a grid).

• AI: a large language model (Claude, via OpenRouter) interprets what each color in a visualization means and chooses a matching sound. AI coding assistance was used during development.

• Audio: instrument and percussion samples from the Philharmonia Orchestra, royalty-free sound effects from Envato, and synthetic sounds created for HEARTH.

• Characters: CC0 3D characters by Quaternius, including a robot with modifications by Don McCurdy.

• Hardware: any computer, phone, or Meta Quest headset. The planned installation adds projection, spatial speakers, and scent, air, and temperature devices.

How it is creative

HEARTH treats scientific images as landscapes to explore as a multisensory experience, adding not only sound but also scents, air currents with different temperatures. Instead of pressing play on a static track, users move through the data and hear it change around them. Our rule sets turn visual features into music rather than noise, so the experience balances scientific interpretation with artistic expression. The installation goes further by adding smell, air, and temperature, turning a data visualization into a place you can step into.

Factors we considered

• Accessibility first: screen-reader support, spoken descriptions, and simple navigation designed for blind and low-vision users. Testing with blind users is the next step.

• Scientific fidelity vs. musicality: sounds follow what each visualization shows (its colors, where they are, and how dense they are), shaped by musical scales and chords so the result is pleasant to hear.

• Reach: a lightweight web app that runs in any modern browser, and also in VR.

• Licensing and attribution: sounds, characters, and libraries are credited with their licenses, and HEARTH makes clear it is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

• Scalability: any SVS visualization that includes a still image can be loaded by its ID, and the same system can grow into a physical installation.
